title: Wolves
synopsis: Two fixers, one body, one Manhattan night. Neither of you was supposed to be assigned to this job. Now you're both here, and the clock is small and meaningless and beautiful.

nodes.text: The body is exactly where the call described. So is the second fixer — a man named Park you have heard about but never met. You both stare. He says, 'I thought I was alone on this.'

choices.text: Refuse to share the job
Accept the buddy and split it

nodes.text: Park, on his burner, calls his guy. You call yours. Both bosses say, 'Do the job.' Neither will admit to the double-dispatch. You and Park look at each other in the elevator mirror.

choices.text: Make a temporary alliance with Park
Pretend to and watch his hands

nodes.text: Park is, you discover, oddly funny — dry as a stone, terrified of yellow taxis, allergic to dogs. He compares spread sheets of corpses he has moved in his career. You realize you have just made a friend, which is the worst.

choices.text: Lean into the partnership
Stay professional, distance everything
choices.consequence: Friendship in this job ends in funerals.

nodes.text: The doorman of the building is alert, awake, and named Mickey. He has seen you both. He is also, suspiciously, willing to be helpful in ways that do not require a tip.

choices.text: Bribe Mickey for the camera tape
Walk Mickey through a story he'll repeat

nodes.text: The penthouse owner — Pamela — returns home unexpectedly. She walks in with grocery bags and a face that has done this once before. 'Again?' she sighs.

choices.text: Recruit Pamela to help
Sedate Pamela politely

nodes.text: Park has a van. You have a freight elevator code. Mickey conveniently looks the other way as you wheel out a 'rolled-up rug.' It is 3:14 a.m. and Manhattan is the wrong city to do this in.

choices.text: Drive to the Hudson
Drive to a friend's freezer truck in the meatpacking district

nodes.text: Park's phone rings — his daughter, 17, can't sleep. He puts her on speaker, casually, while you are mid-cleanup. You realize you have never heard a fixer be a father.

choices.text: Stay quiet while he parents
Take over the floor work so he can take the call properly

nodes.text: A traffic stop. The officer is twenty-three, bored, and decent. Park makes small talk in fluent New Jersey. You hand over a registration that, on paper, will check out. Probably.

choices.text: Talk your way past
Pay the cop a bribe respectfully

nodes.text: A man with three dachshunds walks past the van. He looks too long. Park, who is allergic, sneezes and the door swings.

choices.text: Befriend the dog walker quickly
Drive away before he processes

nodes.text: Your boss calls again. He admits — finally — that the double-dispatch was on purpose. One of you was supposed to take care of the other one, after.

choices.text: Tell Park immediately
Plan to flip on your boss without telling Park

nodes.text: Pamela calls — calmly, after the fact — and offers you both a deal. She has been collecting evidence on the man who employed her to host these meetings. She is, in a real sense, your way out.

choices.text: Take Pamela's deal
choices.consequence: Sometimes a hostess is the boss.

choices.text: Refuse and disappear

nodes.text: 5:11 a.m. A diner that smells like every diner you have ever loved. You and Park, both alive, both a little soot-stained, both eating eggs. The waitress refills your coffee without asking.

choices.text: Plan the rest of the night together
Eat in companionable silence
choices.consequence: Some bonds don't need a strategy.

nodes.text: You drive into the Lincoln Tunnel alone. The boss texts. You don't open it. The yellow lights blur. You become, briefly, a person who is choosing his own next sentence.

choices.text: Drive to your sister's house in Queens
Drive west, indefinitely

nodes.text: You and Park spring the trap on your bosses — together. Pamela helps. Mickey helps. The dog walker is, hilariously, a retired federal agent who helps too. The morning ends with two bosses in custody and a story nobody will believe.

choices.text: Take the deal the feds offer
Refuse the deal; vanish on your own terms

nodes.text: Somewhere in Pennsylvania you stop for coffee at a roadside place. A waitress smiles at you and you realize you are, possibly, allowed to start over.

choices.text: Stay in this town for a season
Keep driving until you find the right town

nodes.text: They give you a new name in a quiet city. You and Park, somehow, get adjacent towns. You meet on Tuesdays in a diner halfway between for eggs and coffee and the pretense of normal lives.

choices.text: Live the small life
Discreetly help people who need fixers, ethically
choices.consequence: Even a small life can serve.

nodes.text: You and Park, off-grid, buy a cabin you have no business owning. He fixes the roof. You teach yourself to make bread. The dog walker visits sometimes. Pamela sends Christmas cards. Mickey, baffling, sends Easter cards only.

choices.text: Stay until you grow old
Go out once more for one good cause

nodes.text: You wander into a small-town hardware store that's hiring. The owner is older than the store. You realize that whatever happens next, your hands still know how to make things work.

choices.text: Take the job here, name on a paycheck
Keep moving — somewhere is still ahead

nodes.text: Park slides into the booth with a folded newspaper and the calm of a man who has, against all odds, achieved Tuesday. You decide together what 'normal' means this week.

choices.text: Just be normal — eggs, paper, no work
Whisper about a case you could quietly help on

nodes.text: Bees in the lavender. Park reading on the porch. A phone you almost never use. You realize the only debt you have left is to yourself — and even that, almost paid.

choices.text: Stay; this is the ending you chose
Take one careful last call — only if it's clean

nodes.text: You stay in the small town and become, eventually, a person who fixes things that aren't bodies. Doors, furnaces, the school's drainage. The town accepts you the way small towns do — slowly, then completely.

You drive for two years. You read every diner menu in America. You become the kind of person who knows when a town will fit and when it won't. One spring you stop. The town is fine. You are fine. The road, finally, lets you.
Park's daughter graduates. He cries into his coffee. You toast with cheap mugs. You are not, by any government's definition, alive. You have, perhaps for the first time, a life.
You and Park become the quiet help — for women leaving bad marriages, for whistleblowers needing rides, for a witness needing a Wednesday. You do not call it justice. You call it the work.
Two old fixers, a wood stove, a dog Park finally tolerates. You both live longer than your old boss would have predicted. You are, against every actuarial table, content.

You go back once, for a thing that needed doing. Park drives. You sit. The job ends cleanly. You return to the cabin a little tired and entirely yourselves. There is no next time. Both of you know it. Both of you are okay.
